title: The Counter-Reformation and the Wars of Religion
subtitle: Rome's answer to the Protestant break, told fairly. Trent and the Jesuits, the saints of a real renewal, and the century of blood from the French massacres to Westphalia that ended Christendom.

sections.title: Two Tellings, Both Flattering
sections.body:
Protestants have often told the Counter-Reformation as a villain's tale, Rome striking back at the recovered gospel with inquisitors and armies. Catholics have often told it as pure renewal, a church cleansing itself of abuses that a few rebels had blown into schism. Both tellings flatter the teller, and neither survives the record. The Catholic Church of the late sixteenth century carried out one of the deepest reforms in its long history, produced saints any tradition should be glad to claim, and planted its faith on continents most reformers barely thought about. And the same era drowned Europe in wars of religion that ended with Christendom itself bleeding out on German fields.

This essay holds both stories, because they are one story. The renewal and the violence flowed from the same conviction, held on every side of the divide, that the truth of God could and should be secured by the power of the state. Catholics believed it. Lutherans believed it. The Reformed believed it. Almost no one in Europe yet doubted it except the hunted Anabaptists, who paid for their doubt with their lives.

So the reader should expect two feelings that do not resolve. Real admiration for Ignatius and Teresa and the reforming bishops who rebuilt a corrupted church, and real horror at Magdeburg and the Paris streets in August of 1572. If only one of those feelings arrives, the story has not been told fairly, and telling it fairly is the whole point. The people on every side were baptized. That is what makes the century unbearable, and what makes it ours.

sections.title: Trent Rebuilds the Old Church
sections.body:
The Council of Trent met in three periods between 1545 and 1563, under three popes, in a small city on the Alpine edge of Italy chosen so that the emperor's men and the pope's men could both reach it. Some thirty bishops attended the opening session, a modest beginning for the most consequential Catholic gathering between the Middle Ages and the twentieth century. Trent answered the Reformation in two registers at once, and fairness requires keeping both in view.

Doctrinally, it drew lines. Against the reformers it declared that justification comes by grace but not by faith alone, that Scripture and the church's unwritten traditions are received with equal reverence, that the sacraments number seven, and that the Mass is a true sacrifice. Whatever a Protestant makes of those judgments, they were not evasions. Trent stated the Catholic position with a clarity the previous century's popes never attempted, and the two sides at last knew exactly where they differed.

Practically, it cleaned house. Bishops were ordered to live in their dioceses and preach in person. Every diocese was ordered to build a seminary, so that priests would be trained men rather than the half-literate placeholders Luther had grown up under. The professional pardon sellers whose trade had lit the fuse in 1517 were abolished. The reforms took decades to bite, but they bit. The Catholic Church that emerged from Trent was more disciplined, more educated, and more serious than the church that had provoked Luther, and it held that shape for four hundred years. Honesty requires a Protestant to say so plainly. Rome did reform, and the reform was real.

sections.title: Ignatius, Xavier, Teresa
sections.body:
The renewal had faces, and they were not mainly the council's. Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque soldier shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona in 1521, read the lives of Christ and the saints in his convalescent bed and came out changed. The Society of Jesus he founded, approved in 1540, took education and mission as its weapons, and by his death in 1556 it counted a thousand men and dozens of colleges. Francis Xavier, one of his first companions, reached India in 1542 and Japan in 1549 and died in 1552 within sight of China, having written home of baptizing until his arms were weary. A generation later Matteo Ricci entered China as a scholar, learned the language and the classics, and won a hearing in Beijing that no gunboat could have won.

In Spain, Teresa of Avila began reforming the Carmelite convents in 1562, joined by John of the Cross, and between them they wrote some of the deepest Christian books on prayer ever produced. In Milan, Charles Borromeo showed what a Trent bishop looked like, building seminaries and serving his plague-struck city in person in 1576. This was not reaction. It was holiness, and Protestants should be able to say so without flinching.

And the same renewal had a fist. The Roman Inquisition was founded in 1542, the Index of Forbidden Books in 1559, and the machinery that disciplined wayward clergy also silenced honest questions, condemning Galileo as late as 1633. Renewal and repression were not opposites in this church. They were the same energy, applied with the same seriousness, and no account is honest that keeps one and drops the other.

sections.title: France, the Netherlands, and the Massacres
sections.body:
The wars came first to France, where the Reformed minority, the Huguenots, had grown too large to crush and too hated to tolerate. From 1562 the country fell in and out of civil war for nearly four decades, and the worst of it has a date. On Saint Bartholomew's Day, in August of 1572, the Huguenot leadership was murdered in Paris, and the killing spread through the streets and out into the provinces for weeks. Thousands died, historians still argue how many thousands, and Rome, hearing the news as the suppression of a treasonous plot, celebrated with a sung Te Deum and a commemorative medal. Catholic historians record that celebration today with shame, which is itself a kind of progress.

Peace of a sort came when Henry of Navarre, the Protestant heir, judged the crown worth a conversion, became Catholic, and in 1598 issued the Edict of Nantes, granting the Huguenots limited toleration. It lasted less than a century. Louis the Fourteenth revoked it in 1685, and hundreds of thousands of France's most industrious subjects fled the country.

In the Low Countries, Calvinist rebels fought Catholic Spain for eighty years, and Spain's Council of Troubles executed more than a thousand people in a campaign its victims called the Council of Blood. And lest the ledger look one-sided, Protestant England in the same decades hanged and quartered Catholic priests as traitors. Every confession with power used it. The parties differed over grace and sacraments. Over the sword they hardly differed at all, and that agreement is the century's real indictment.

sections.title: The Thirty Years War
sections.body:
The catastrophe began in Prague in May of 1618, when Protestant nobles threw two imperial officials and their secretary out of a castle window. The three men survived the seventy-foot fall. Catholic pamphlets credited angels, Protestant pamphlets credited a dung heap, and Europe laughed its way into the abyss. What followed drew in Bohemia, the German lands, Denmark, Sweden, Spain, and France, in a war that began over religion and ended as something colder.

The name to know is Magdeburg. In May of 1631 imperial troops stormed the Protestant city, and in the sack and fire that followed, some twenty thousand of its twenty-five thousand people died. The city's name became a byword across Europe for what armies do. The Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus, hailed by Protestants as their deliverer, won his battles and died in the fog at Lutzen in 1632, and the war ground on without him. By its later years the fig leaf had dropped entirely. Catholic France, guided by a cardinal, was financing Lutheran Sweden against the Catholic emperor, because the logic of state had swallowed the logic of confession.

The cost fell on people who had never read a theologian. Armies lived off the land, and plague and famine marched with them. The German lands lost perhaps a fifth of their entire population, and some regions lost half. Historians still argue the figures. None argue the desolation. Whatever each side believed it was defending in 1618, by 1648 the argument lay buried under a generation of the baptized dead.

sections.title: What Westphalia Ended
sections.body:
Peace came in 1648, in the twin treaties signed at Munster and Osnabruck that history calls the Peace of Westphalia, and it is worth noticing what kind of peace it was. Nobody had won. The settlement fixed the confessional map roughly where exhaustion had left it, confirmed the principle inherited from Augsburg in 1555 that a territory's ruler set its religion, and admitted the Reformed churches to the arrangement alongside Lutherans and Catholics. Dissenting subjects received narrow protections and the right to emigrate. It was not toleration as we mean the word. It was a truce between exhausted certainties.

Pope Innocent the Tenth condemned the settlement as null and void. The Catholic powers signed anyway, and nothing happened, and that nothing was the loudest sound in Europe. For a thousand years the church had claimed some authority over the ordering of Christian nations. After 1648 the nations ordered themselves, and religion began its long move from public order to state policy to private conscience. Textbooks long dated the modern state system from these treaties, and though historians now qualify the claim, something real did end there. Christendom, the dream of Europe as a single Christian house, did not survive the wars fought to decide who owned the house.

And here is the weight the church still carries. The wars were not fought by skeptics. They were fought by baptized men, certain God was with them, and modern European unbelief was born in no small part from watching them. When a skeptic says Christianity means violence, this is the century he is remembering. The honest answer has never been denial. It is grief, and the long labor of being a different kind of church.

keyFigures.name: Ignatius of Loyola
keyFigures.note: Wounded soldier who founded the Society of Jesus, approved in 1540.

keyFigures.name: Francis Xavier
keyFigures.note: Jesuit missionary to India and Japan, dead within sight of China in 1552.

keyFigures.name: Teresa of Avila
keyFigures.note: Reformer of the Carmelites and one of the church's great teachers of prayer.

keyFigures.name: Charles Borromeo
keyFigures.note: Archbishop of Milan who embodied the reforming bishop Trent imagined.

keyFigures.name: Henry the Fourth of France
keyFigures.note: The Protestant heir whose conversion and Edict of Nantes paused the French wars.

keyFigures.name: Gustavus Adolphus
keyFigures.note: Swedish king and Protestant champion, killed in battle at Lutzen in 1632.
